questions.stem: The word 'Renaissance' comes from French. What does it mean?
options: Discovery
Revolution
Rebirth
Reform
questions.explanation: Renaissance means 'rebirth': people of the time felt they were reviving the learning and art of ancient Greece and Rome. 'Reform' is linked with the Reformation, a religious movement that came out of the same period but is a separate idea.

questions.stem: Why did the Renaissance begin in Italy?
options: Italy was a single united kingdom ruled by one powerful king
Italy had escaped the Black Death while the rest of Europe suffered badly
The printing press had first been invented in the city of Florence
Its trading cities were wealthy and full of reminders of ancient Rome
questions.explanation: Italian city-states such as Florence and Venice grew rich from trade and banking, and Roman ruins and manuscripts surrounded them, inspiring interest in the classical past. Italy was not united until 1861 — it was a patchwork of rival states — and Florence was hit very hard by the Black Death.

questions.stem: Which family of bankers dominated Florence for much of the 1400s and paid for many great works of art?
options: The Habsburgs
The Medici
The Sforza
The Tudors
questions.explanation: The Medici bank made the family enormously rich, and leaders such as Cosimo and Lorenzo the Magnificent used that wealth to dominate Florence's government and support artists and scholars. The Sforza ruled Milan, a rival state.

questions.stem: In Renaissance Italy, what was a patron?
options: A wealthy person or group who paid artists to create works
An apprentice who ground and mixed paints in a workshop
A guild official who set the price of every painting sold
A Church inspector who judged which artworks were heretical
questions.explanation: Patrons — rich families, guilds, popes and city governments — commissioned and paid for paintings, sculptures and buildings, often to show their wealth, faith and power. Apprentices worked in an artist's workshop learning the trade; they did not pay for the art.

options: A style of painting that showed people as flat figures on gold
A movement that studied Greek and Roman writers and valued human ability
A belief that educated people should reject religion and the Church completely
A system of farming in which peasants owned the land they worked
questions.explanation: Humanists studied classical texts in subjects such as history, poetry and ethics, and stressed what educated individuals could achieve. Most humanists were sincere Christians, so humanism was not a rejection of religion, even if it shifted attention towards life in this world.

questions.stem: Which technique did Renaissance artists use to make flat paintings look three-dimensional?
options: Gold-leaf backgrounds that made the figures stand out sharply
Painting every figure the same size whatever its distance
Outlining every object with thick, dark lines of black paint
Linear perspective, with lines meeting at a vanishing point
questions.explanation: Brunelleschi worked out the rules of linear perspective in Florence in the early 1400s: parallel lines are drawn meeting at a vanishing point, so objects shrink as they recede. Flat gold backgrounds were typical of medieval religious art, which Renaissance painters moved away from.

questions.stem: Who designed the huge dome of Florence Cathedral, completed in the 1430s?
options: Michelangelo Buonarroti
Leonardo da Vinci
Niccolò Machiavelli
Filippo Brunelleschi
questions.explanation: Brunelleschi solved the problem of roofing the cathedral's vast crossing with a double-shelled brick dome built without a wooden frame underneath. Michelangelo designed the dome of St Peter's in Rome over a century later, which is why the two are often confused.

questions.stem: Which artist painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel in Rome and carved the marble statue of David?
options: Raphael
Titian
Michelangelo
Leonardo da Vinci
questions.explanation: Michelangelo carved David between 1501 and 1504 and painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling for Pope Julius II between 1508 and 1512. Leonardo da Vinci painted the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper but did not work on the Sistine Chapel.

questions.stem: Leonardo da Vinci is often called a 'Renaissance man' because he:
options: worked as a painter, engineer and inventor, and studied anatomy
was the first artist ever to be paid by the Medici family
started the Renaissance by rediscovering lost Greek texts
ruled Milan as its duke and paid many artists to work there
questions.explanation: A 'Renaissance man' is someone skilled in many fields, and Leonardo's notebooks are full of anatomy drawings, machines and studies of nature alongside his paintings. He worked for the Sforza dukes of Milan, but he was never a ruler himself.

questions.stem: Machiavelli's book The Prince (written in 1513) is famous for arguing that:
options: a ruler should always be honest and merciful, even if it costs him his state
the pope should rule the whole of Italy as its single king
ordinary citizens should elect a new ruler every single year
a ruler may have to be ruthless to keep power and the state secure
questions.explanation: Machiavelli advised that a prince should be prepared to deceive or use force when needed, judging actions by their results; it is safer, he wrote, to be feared than loved if one cannot be both. This is why 'Machiavellian' now describes cunning, ruthless behaviour — the opposite of always being honest.

questions.stem: What was the elected leader of the Republic of Venice called?
options: The doge
The caliph
The tsar
The jarl
questions.explanation: Venice was a republic led by a doge, elected for life from the city's noble families, whose names were recorded in the Libro d'Oro (Golden Book). A caliph was a Muslim ruler, and a tsar was the ruler of Russia.

questions.stem: In Renaissance Florence, who were the popolo grasso ('fat people')?
options: Monks and nuns living in the monasteries of the city
Noble knights who owned castles out in the countryside
Wealthy merchants, bankers and members of the major guilds
Poor wool workers and labourers who had no guild of their own
questions.explanation: The popolo grasso were the rich commercial families who controlled the major guilds and the city's government. The poor workers, such as the wool carders, were the popolo minuto ('little people'), who rose up in the Ciompi revolt of 1378.

questions.stem: How did Gutenberg's printing press, developed around 1450, help spread Renaissance ideas?
options: Monks were given more time to copy books neatly by hand
Books became rarer, so new ideas were guarded more carefully
Books could be produced quickly and cheaply in large numbers
Books could be printed only in Latin, which united all scholars
questions.explanation: Movable-type printing made books far cheaper and more plentiful, so humanist writings, classical texts and new ideas travelled across Europe, helping the Renaissance spread north to places such as England. Printers soon produced books in everyday languages as well as Latin.

questions.stem: Which woman was a celebrated Renaissance patron and collector, and governed Mantua while her husband was away?
options: Elizabeth I
Catherine the Great
Isabella d'Este
Joan of Arc
questions.explanation: Isabella d'Este, Marchesa of Mantua, collected art and antiquities, supported painters and writers, and ran the state during her husband's absences. Joan of Arc lived in France in the early 1400s, and Catherine the Great ruled Russia in the 1700s.

questions.stem: How did the fall of Constantinople to the Ottoman Turks in 1453 add to the Renaissance in Italy?
options: Italian armies captured the city and took its libraries home
The Byzantine emperor moved his court and capital to Florence
Crusaders recaptured the city and shared its treasures with Italy
Greek scholars fled west to Italy, bringing ancient manuscripts
questions.explanation: Greek-speaking scholars had been coming to Italy for decades, and after 1453 more arrived with manuscripts of Greek writers such as Plato, strengthening the study of Greek. The Ottomans held the city from 1453 onwards, so no Italian or crusader army took it.

questions.stem: Michelangelo's David was placed outside Florence's town hall in 1504, while the Medici were in exile. Many historians see it as a symbol of:
options: the triumph of the Medici, who had just returned to rule the city
the defeat of Florence by the armies of the King of France
the Florentine Republic standing firm against more powerful enemies
the pope's power over the city of Florence and all of its rulers
questions.explanation: David, the young hero who beat the giant Goliath, was placed outside the seat of the republic's government, where it was read as Florence defending its liberty against stronger rivals. The Medici had been expelled in 1494 and did not return until 1512, so it could not celebrate their return.

questions.stem: In 1860 the historian Jacob Burckhardt described the Renaissance as a sharp break from the Middle Ages. What do many historians argue today?
options: Much continued from the Middle Ages, which had kept classical learning alive
The Renaissance was invented in the 1800s and produced no real works of art at all
The Renaissance began in England and reached Italy only a century later
The break was even sharper, since medieval people had no books at all
questions.explanation: Historians now stress continuity: medieval monks, scholars and universities had already copied and studied many classical texts, and there were earlier 'renaissances' such as the twelfth-century revival of learning. The idea that medieval people had no books ignores centuries of manuscripts, libraries and universities.

questions.stem: Which Italian state was ruled directly by the pope?
options: The Duchy of Milan
The Kingdom of Naples
The Papal States
The Republic of Venice
questions.explanation: The popes ruled the Papal States, a band of territory across central Italy centred on Rome, as kings as well as Church leaders. Naples was a monarchy, Milan a duchy ruled by the Visconti and then the Sforza, and Venice a republic led by a doge.

questions.stem: Florence's Catasto of 1427 recorded the property, debts and household members of families across the city for tax. Why is it so valuable to historians?
options: It lists every painting and sculpture made in Florence in that year
It is the only surviving record of the Black Death in Florence
It reveals the wealth and households of ordinary families, not only the elite
It records the private thoughts and plans of the Medici family leaders
questions.explanation: Because nearly every household had to declare what it owned and who lived in it, the Catasto lets historians study wealth, family size and work across the whole city, including people who left no other records. It is a tax survey, so it says little about the private thoughts of the powerful.
